# wmi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wmi/latest/target-redirect/i686-pc-windows-msvc/wmi/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#wmi-rs)WMI-rs

[WMI](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/wmisdk/about-wmi) is a management API for Windows-based operating systems.
This crate provides both a high-level Rust API (focused on data retrieval, event queries and method execution),
as well as a mid-level API for easy access to native WMI methods.

This crate also uses `serde` for transforming between native WMI class objects and plain Rust structs.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

Before using WMI, a connection must be created.

```
use wmi::WMIConnection;
let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
```
There are multiple ways to get data from the OS using this crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-variants)Operating on untyped `Variant`s

WMI data model is based on COM’s [ VARIANT](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/oaidl/ns-oaidl-tagvariant) Type, which is a struct capable of holding
many types of data.

This crate provides the analogous [`wmi::Variant`] enum.

Using this enum, we can execute a simple WMI query and inspect the results.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use wmi::*;
let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use wmi::Variant;
let results: Vec<HashMap<String, Variant>> = wmi_con.raw_query("SELECT * FROM Win32_OperatingSystem").unwrap();
for os in results {
    println!("{:#?}", os);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-strongly-typed-data-structures)Using strongly typed data structures

Using `serde`, it is possible to return a struct representing the the data.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::Deserialize;
use wmi::WMIDateTime;
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_OperatingSystem")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct OperatingSystem {
    caption: String,
    debug: bool,
    last_boot_up_time: WMIDateTime,
}
let results: Vec<OperatingSystem> = wmi_con.query()?;
for os in results {
    println!("{:#?}", os);
}
```
Because the name of the struct given to `serde` matches the [WMI class](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/cimwin32prov/win32-operatingsystem) name, the SQL query
can be inferred.

[§](https://docs.rs#high-level-api-functions)High-level API functions

Queries and data retrieval - [ WMIConnection::query](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.query),

[,](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.filtered_query)

`WMIConnection::filtered_query`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.get)

`WMIConnection::get`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.get_by_path)

`WMIConnection::get_by_path`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.associators)

`WMIConnection::associators`Event listening - [ WMIConnection::notification](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.notification) and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.filtered_notification)

`WMIConnection::filtered_notification`Method calling - [ WMIConnection::exec_class_method](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.exec_class_method) and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.exec_instance_method)

`WMIConnection::exec_instance_method`Most of these have `async` versions as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#mid-level-api-functions)Mid-level API functions

Queries and data retrieval - [ WMIConnection::get_object](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.get_object),

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.exec_query)

`WMIConnection::exec_query`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.exec_query_async)

`WMIConnection::exec_query_async`Event listening - [ WMIConnection::exec_notification_query](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.exec_notification_query) and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.exec_notification_query_async)

`WMIConnection::exec_notification_query_async`Method calling - [ WMIConnection::exec_method](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.exec_method) and

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.IWbemClassWrapper.html)

`IWbemClassWrapper`These try to keep the names of the underlying WMI machinery.

[§](https://docs.rs#subscribing-to-event-notifications)Subscribing to event notifications

Using this crate you can subscribe to events notifications generated upon changes in WMI data and services.

When querying for events, it is important to remember there are two types of event notifications.

The first one is notifications about changes to the standard WMI data models. They are called **intrinsic events**.

Events like [ __InstanceCreationEvent](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--instancecreationevent) or

[are examples of such events.](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--namespacedeletionevent)

`__NamespaceDeletionEvent`The second type is notifications about changes made by providers. They are called **extrinsic events**.

Any WMI class deriving from the [ __ExtrinsicEvent](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--extrinsicevent) class is an extrinsic event.

An example of such events are

[and](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/desktop/krnlprov/win32-processstarttrace)

`Win32_ProcessStartTrace`[classes.](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/cimwin32prov/win32-volumechangeevent)

`Win32_VolumeChangeEvent`For more information about event queries, [see here](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/receiving-a-wmi-event#event-queries).

You can use [WMI Code Creator](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/download/details.aspx?id=8572) to see available events and create queries for them.

The [ notification](https://docs.rs/connection/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.notification) method returns an iterator that waits for any incoming events
resulting from the provided query. Loops reading from this iterator will not end until they are broken.

An example of subscribing to an intrinsic event notification for every new `Win32_Process`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "__InstanceCreationEvent")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct NewProcessEvent {
    target_instance: Process
}
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_Process")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct Process {
    process_id: u32,
    name: String,
    executable_path: Option<String>,
}
let mut filters = HashMap::<String, FilterValue>::new();
filters.insert("TargetInstance".to_owned(), FilterValue::is_a::<Process>()?);
let iterator = wmi_con.filtered_notification::<NewProcessEvent>(&filters, Some(Duration::from_secs(1)))?;
for result in iterator {
    let process = result?.target_instance;
    println!("New process!");
    println!("PID:        {}", process.process_id);
    println!("Name:       {}", process.name);
    println!("Executable: {:?}", process.executable_path);
} // Loop will end only on error
```
An example of subscribing to an extrinsic event notification `Win32_ProcessStartTrace`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_ProcessStartTrace")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct ProcessStartTrace {
    process_id: u32,
    process_name: String,
}
let iterator = wmi_con.notification::<ProcessStartTrace>()?;
for result in iterator {
    let trace = result?;
    println!("Process started!");
    println!("PID:  {}", trace.process_id);
    println!("Name: {}", trace.process_name);
} // Loop will end only on error
```
[§](https://docs.rs#executing-methods)Executing Methods

The crate also offers support for executing WMI methods on classes and instances.

See [ WMIConnection::exec_class_method](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.exec_class_method),

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.exec_instance_method)

`WMIConnection::exec_instance_method`[for detailed examples.](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.exec_method)

`WMIConnection::exec_method`[§](https://docs.rs#custom-authentication-levels)Custom Authentication Levels

Some WMI namespaces require specific authentication levels when accessing
sensitive system information. Use [ WMIConnection::set_proxy_blanket](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.set_proxy_blanket) to configure this,
which maps directly to the Windows

[function.](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/combaseapi/nf-combaseapi-cosetproxyblanket)

`CoSetProxyBlanket`**Default Behavior**:

- Local connections: `AuthLevel::Call`
- Remote connections: `AuthLevel::PktPrivacy`

```
use serde::Deserialize;
// Access BitLocker data, which requires packet-level encryption.
// Note: admin privileges are required for BitLocker queries.
let wmi_con = WMIConnection::with_namespace_path(
    "ROOT\\CIMV2\\Security\\MicrosoftVolumeEncryption"
)?;
wmi_con.set_proxy_blanket(AuthLevel::PktPrivacy)?;
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_EncryptableVolume")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct EncryptableVolume {
    device_id: String,
    protection_status: Option<u32>,  // 0=Unprotected, 1=Protected, 2=Unknown
}
let volumes: Vec<EncryptableVolume> = wmi_con.query()?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#internals)Internals

[ WMIConnection](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html) is used to create and execute a WMI query, returning

[which is a wrapper for a WMI object pointer.](https://docs.rs/struct.IWbemClassWrapper.html)

`IWbemClassWrapper`Then, `from_wbem_class_obj` is used to create a Rust struct with the equivalent data.

Deserializing data from WMI and into Rust is done via `serde`.
More info can be found in `serde`’s documentation about [writing a data format](https://serde.rs/data-format.html).
The deserializer will either use the field names defined on the output struct,
or retrieve all field names from WMI if the output is a `HashMap`.

There are two main data structures (other than pointers to object) which convert native data to Rust data structures:
[ crate::Variant](https://docs.rs/enum.Variant.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/safearray/struct.SafeArrayAccessor.html)

`SafeArrayAccessor`Most native objects has an equivalent wrapper struct which implements `Drop` for that data.

[§](https://docs.rs#async-query)Async Query

Async queries use WMI’s native async support (but a runtime like `tokio`, `async-std` or `futures::executor::block_on` is still required).

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use wmi::*;
let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
use serde::Deserialize;
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_OperatingSystem")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct OperatingSystem {
    caption: String,
    debug: bool,
}
let results: Vec<OperatingSystem> = wmi_con.async_query().await?;
for os in results {
    println!("{:#?}", os);
}
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [IWbem](https://docs.rs/struct.IWbemClassWrapper.html)- Class - Wrapper
- A wrapper around a [IWbemClassObject](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wbemcli/nn-wbemcli-iwbemclassobject).
- [WMIConnection](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html)
- A connection to the local WMI provider.
- [WMIContext](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIContext.html)
- Provides access to WMI’s context, available via `WMIConnection::ctx`
- [WMIDate](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIDateTime.html)- Time
- A wrapper type around `chrono`’s`DateTime`(if the`chrono`feature is active. ), which supports parsing from WMI-format strings.
- [WMIDuration](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIDuration.html)
- A wrapper type around Duration, which supports parsing from WMI-format strings.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Auth](https://docs.rs/enum.AuthLevel.html)- Level
- Authentication level for a WMI connection proxy, passed to `CoSetProxyBlanket`
- [Context](https://docs.rs/enum.ContextValueType.html)- Value - Type
- [Filter](https://docs.rs/enum.FilterValue.html)- Value
- [Variant](https://docs.rs/enum.Variant.html)
- [WMIError](https://docs.rs/enum.WMIError.html)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_notification_query.html)- notification_ - query
- Build an SQL query for an event notification subscription with the given filters and within polling time, over the given type (using its fields). For example, for:
- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_query.html)- query
- Build an SQL query for the given filters, over the given type (using its name and fields). For example, for:
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/fn.quote_and_escape_wql_str.html)- and_ - escape_ - wql_ - str
- Quote/escape a string for WQL.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [WMIResult](https://docs.rs/type.WMIResult.html)
- Alias type for `Result<T, WMIError>`

- [WMIDate](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIDateTime.html)- Time
- A wrapper type around `chrono`’s`DateTime`(if the`chrono`feature is active. ), which supports parsing from WMI-format strings.
- [WMIDuration](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIDuration.html)
- A wrapper type around Duration, which supports parsing from WMI-format strings.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Auth](https://docs.rs/enum.AuthLevel.html)- Level
- Authentication level for a WMI connection proxy, passed to `CoSetProxyBlanket`
- [Context](https://docs.rs/enum.ContextValueType.html)- Value - Type
- [Filter](https://docs.rs/enum.FilterValue.html)- Value
- [Variant](https://docs.rs/enum.Variant.html)
- [WMIError](https://docs.rs/enum.WMIError.html)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_notification_query.html)- notification_ - query
- Build an SQL query for an event notification subscription with the given filters and within polling time, over the given type (using its fields). For example, for:
- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_query.html)- query
- Build an SQL query for the given filters, over the given type (using its name and fields). For example, for:
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/fn.quote_and_escape_wql_str.html)- and_ - escape_ - wql_ - str
- Quote/escape a string for WQL.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [WMIResult](https://docs.rs/type.WMIResult.html)
- Alias type for `Result<T, WMIError>`

# wmi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wmi/latest/target-redirect/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/wmi/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#wmi-rs)WMI-rs

[WMI](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/wmisdk/about-wmi) is a management API for Windows-based operating systems.
This crate provides both a high-level Rust API (focused on data retrieval, event queries and method execution),
as well as a mid-level API for easy access to native WMI methods.

This crate also uses `serde` for transforming between native WMI class objects and plain Rust structs.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

Before using WMI, a connection must be created.

```
use wmi::WMIConnection;
let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
```
There are multiple ways to get data from the OS using this crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-variants)Operating on untyped `Variant`s

WMI data model is based on COM’s [ VARIANT](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/oaidl/ns-oaidl-tagvariant) Type, which is a struct capable of holding
many types of data.

This crate provides the analogous [`wmi::Variant`] enum.

Using this enum, we can execute a simple WMI query and inspect the results.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use wmi::*;
let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use wmi::Variant;
let results: Vec<HashMap<String, Variant>> = wmi_con.raw_query("SELECT * FROM Win32_OperatingSystem").unwrap();
for os in results {
    println!("{:#?}", os);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-strongly-typed-data-structures)Using strongly typed data structures

Using `serde`, it is possible to return a struct representing the the data.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::Deserialize;
use wmi::WMIDateTime;
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_OperatingSystem")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct OperatingSystem {
    caption: String,
    debug: bool,
    last_boot_up_time: WMIDateTime,
}
let results: Vec<OperatingSystem> = wmi_con.query()?;
for os in results {
    println!("{:#?}", os);
}
```
Because the name of the struct given to `serde` matches the [WMI class](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/cimwin32prov/win32-operatingsystem) name, the SQL query
can be inferred.

[§](https://docs.rs#high-level-api-functions)High-level API functions

Queries and data retrieval - [`WMIConnection::query`], [`WMIConnection::filtered_query`], [`WMIConnection::get`], [`WMIConnection::get_by_path`] and [`WMIConnection::associators`].

Event listening - [`WMIConnection::notification`] and [`WMIConnection::filtered_notification`].

Method calling - [`WMIConnection::exec_class_method`] and [`WMIConnection::exec_instance_method`].

Most of these have `async` versions as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#mid-level-api-functions)Mid-level API functions

Queries and data retrieval - [`WMIConnection::get_object`], [`WMIConnection::exec_query`] and [`WMIConnection::exec_query_async`].

Event listening - [`WMIConnection::exec_notification_query`] and [`WMIConnection::exec_notification_query_async`].

Method calling - [`WMIConnection::exec_method`] and [`IWbemClassWrapper`].

These try to keep the names of the underlying WMI machinery.

[§](https://docs.rs#subscribing-to-event-notifications)Subscribing to event notifications

Using this crate you can subscribe to events notifications generated upon changes in WMI data and services.

When querying for events, it is important to remember there are two types of event notifications.

The first one is notifications about changes to the standard WMI data models. They are called **intrinsic events**.

Events like [ __InstanceCreationEvent](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--instancecreationevent) or

[are examples of such events.](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--namespacedeletionevent)

`__NamespaceDeletionEvent`The second type is notifications about changes made by providers. They are called **extrinsic events**.

Any WMI class deriving from the [ __ExtrinsicEvent](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--extrinsicevent) class is an extrinsic event.

An example of such events are

[and](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/desktop/krnlprov/win32-processstarttrace)

`Win32_ProcessStartTrace`[classes.](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/cimwin32prov/win32-volumechangeevent)

`Win32_VolumeChangeEvent`For more information about event queries, [see here](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/receiving-a-wmi-event#event-queries).

You can use [WMI Code Creator](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/download/details.aspx?id=8572) to see available events and create queries for them.

The [ notification](https://docs.rs/connection/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.notification) method returns an iterator that waits for any incoming events
resulting from the provided query. Loops reading from this iterator will not end until they are broken.

An example of subscribing to an intrinsic event notification for every new `Win32_Process`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "__InstanceCreationEvent")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct NewProcessEvent {
    target_instance: Process
}
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_Process")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct Process {
    process_id: u32,
    name: String,
    executable_path: Option<String>,
}
let mut filters = HashMap::<String, FilterValue>::new();
filters.insert("TargetInstance".to_owned(), FilterValue::is_a::<Process>()?);
let iterator = wmi_con.filtered_notification::<NewProcessEvent>(&filters, Some(Duration::from_secs(1)))?;
for result in iterator {
    let process = result?.target_instance;
    println!("New process!");
    println!("PID:        {}", process.process_id);
    println!("Name:       {}", process.name);
    println!("Executable: {:?}", process.executable_path);
} // Loop will end only on error
```
An example of subscribing to an extrinsic event notification `Win32_ProcessStartTrace`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_ProcessStartTrace")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct ProcessStartTrace {
    process_id: u32,
    process_name: String,
}
let iterator = wmi_con.notification::<ProcessStartTrace>()?;
for result in iterator {
    let trace = result?;
    println!("Process started!");
    println!("PID:  {}", trace.process_id);
    println!("Name: {}", trace.process_name);
} // Loop will end only on error
```
[§](https://docs.rs#executing-methods)Executing Methods

The crate also offers support for executing WMI methods on classes and instances.

See [`WMIConnection::exec_class_method`], [`WMIConnection::exec_instance_method`] and [`WMIConnection::exec_method`]
for detailed examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-authentication-levels)Custom Authentication Levels

Some WMI namespaces require specific authentication levels when accessing
sensitive system information. Use [`WMIConnection::set_proxy_blanket`] to configure this,
which maps directly to the Windows [ CoSetProxyBlanket](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/combaseapi/nf-combaseapi-cosetproxyblanket) function.

**Default Behavior**:

- Local connections: [`AuthLevel::Call`] (message authentication)
- Remote connections: [`AuthLevel::PktPrivacy`] (packet encryption)

```
use serde::Deserialize;
// Access BitLocker data, which requires packet-level encryption.
// Note: admin privileges are required for BitLocker queries.
let wmi_con = WMIConnection::with_namespace_path(
    "ROOT\\CIMV2\\Security\\MicrosoftVolumeEncryption"
)?;
wmi_con.set_proxy_blanket(AuthLevel::PktPrivacy)?;
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_EncryptableVolume")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct EncryptableVolume {
    device_id: String,
    protection_status: Option<u32>,  // 0=Unprotected, 1=Protected, 2=Unknown
}
let volumes: Vec<EncryptableVolume> = wmi_con.query()?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#internals)Internals

[`WMIConnection`] is used to create and execute a WMI query, returning
[`IWbemClassWrapper`] which is a wrapper for a WMI object pointer.

Then, `from_wbem_class_obj` is used to create a Rust struct with the equivalent data.

Deserializing data from WMI and into Rust is done via `serde`.
More info can be found in `serde`’s documentation about [writing a data format](https://serde.rs/data-format.html).
The deserializer will either use the field names defined on the output struct,
or retrieve all field names from WMI if the output is a `HashMap`.

There are two main data structures (other than pointers to object) which convert native data to Rust data structures:
[`crate::Variant`] and [ SafeArrayAccessor](safearray::SafeArrayAccessor).

Most native objects has an equivalent wrapper struct which implements `Drop` for that data.

[§](https://docs.rs#async-query)Async Query

Async queries use WMI’s native async support (but a runtime like `tokio`, `async-std` or `futures::executor::block_on` is still required).

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use wmi::*;
let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
use serde::Deserialize;
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_OperatingSystem")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct OperatingSystem {
    caption: String,
    debug: bool,
}
let results: Vec<OperatingSystem> = wmi_con.async_query().await?;
for os in results {
    println!("{:#?}", os);
}
```

---

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/wmi/latest/aarch64-apple-darwin/src/wmi/lib.rs.html

# wmi/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! # WMI-rs
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! [WMI] is a management API for Windows-based operating systems.
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! This crate provides both a high-level Rust API (focused on data retrieval, event queries and method execution),
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! as well as a mid-level API for easy access to native WMI methods.
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! This crate also uses `serde` for transforming between native WMI class objects and plain Rust structs.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! # Quickstart
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! Before using WMI, a connection must be created.
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! ```rust
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! # fn main() -> wmi::WMIResult<()> {
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! use wmi::WMIConnection;
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! #   Ok(())
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! # }
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! ```
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! There are multiple ways to get data from the OS using this crate.
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! ## Operating on untyped `Variant`s
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! WMI data model is based on COM's [`VARIANT`] Type, which is a struct capable of holding
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! many types of data.
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! This crate provides the analogous [`wmi::Variant`] enum.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! Using this enum, we can execute a simple WMI query and inspect the results.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! ```edition2018
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! # fn main() -> wmi::WMIResult<()> {
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! use wmi::*;
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! use std::collections::HashMap;
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! use wmi::Variant;
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! let results: Vec<HashMap<String, Variant>> = wmi_con.raw_query("SELECT * FROM Win32_OperatingSystem").unwrap();
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! for os in results {
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!     println!("{:#?}", os);
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! }
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! #   Ok(())
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! # }
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! ```
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! ## Using strongly typed data structures
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! Using `serde`, it is possible to return a struct representing the the data.
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! ```edition2018
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! # fn main() -> wmi::WMIResult<()> {
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! # use wmi::*;
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! # let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! use serde::Deserialize;
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! # #[cfg(feature = "chrono")]
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! use wmi::WMIDateTime;
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! # #[cfg(all(feature = "time", not(feature = "chrono")))]
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! # use wmi::WMIOffsetDateTime as WMIDateTime;
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! #[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! #[serde(rename = "Win32_OperatingSystem")]
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! #[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! struct OperatingSystem {
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!     caption: String,
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!     debug: bool,
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!     last_boot_up_time: WMIDateTime,
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! }
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! let results: Vec<OperatingSystem> = wmi_con.query()?;
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! for os in results {
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!     println!("{:#?}", os);
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! }
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! #   Ok(())
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! # }
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! ```
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! Because the name of the struct given to `serde` matches the [WMI class] name, the SQL query
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! can be inferred.
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! [WMI]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/wmisdk/about-wmi
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! [Creating a WMI Application Using C++]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/wmisdk/creating-a-wmi-application-using-c-
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! [`VARIANT`]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/oaidl/ns-oaidl-tagvariant
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! [WMI class]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/cimwin32prov/win32-operatingsystem
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! # High-level API functions
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! Queries and data retrieval - [`WMIConnection::query`], [`WMIConnection::filtered_query`], [`WMIConnection::get`], [`WMIConnection::get_by_path`] and [`WMIConnection::associators`].
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! Event listening - [`WMIConnection::notification`] and [`WMIConnection::filtered_notification`].
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! Method calling - [`WMIConnection::exec_class_method`] and [`WMIConnection::exec_instance_method`].
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! Most of these have `async` versions as well.
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! # Mid-level API functions
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! Queries and data retrieval - [`WMIConnection::get_object`], [`WMIConnection::exec_query`] and [`WMIConnection::exec_query_async`].
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! Event listening - [`WMIConnection::exec_notification_query`] and [`WMIConnection::exec_notification_query_async`].
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! Method calling - [`WMIConnection::exec_method`] and [`IWbemClassWrapper`].
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//!
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! These try to keep the names of the underlying WMI machinery.
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! # Subscribing to event notifications
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! Using this crate you can subscribe to events notifications generated upon changes in WMI data and services.
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! When querying for events, it is important to remember there are two types of event notifications. \
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! The first one is notifications about changes to the standard WMI data models. They are called **intrinsic events**. \
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! Events like [`__InstanceCreationEvent`] or [`__NamespaceDeletionEvent`] are examples of such events.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! The second type is notifications about changes made by providers. They are called **extrinsic events**.  \
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! Any WMI class deriving from the [`__ExtrinsicEvent`] class is an extrinsic event. \
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! An example of such events are [`Win32_ProcessStartTrace`] and [`Win32_VolumeChangeEvent`] classes.
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! For more information about event queries, [see here](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/receiving-a-wmi-event#event-queries).\
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! You can use [WMI Code Creator] to see available events and create queries for them.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! The [`notification`] method returns an iterator that waits for any incoming events
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! resulting from the provided query. Loops reading from this iterator will not end until they are broken.
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! An example of subscribing to an intrinsic event notification for every new [`Win32_Process`]
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! ```edition2018
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! # use wmi::*;
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! # #[cfg(not(feature = "test"))]
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! # fn main() {}
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! # #[cfg(feature = "test")]
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! # fn main() -> WMIResult<()>{
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! # use serde::Deserialize;
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! # use std::{collections::HashMap, time::Duration};
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! # let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! #[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! #[serde(rename = "__InstanceCreationEvent")]
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! #[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! struct NewProcessEvent {
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!     target_instance: Process
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! }
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! #[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! #[serde(rename = "Win32_Process")]
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! #[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! struct Process {
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!     process_id: u32,
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!     name: String,
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//!     executable_path: Option<String>,
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! }
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! let mut filters = HashMap::<String, FilterValue>::new();
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! filters.insert("TargetInstance".to_owned(), FilterValue::is_a::<Process>()?);
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! let iterator = wmi_con.filtered_notification::<NewProcessEvent>(&filters, Some(Duration::from_secs(1)))?;
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! # tests::start_test_program();
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! for result in iterator {
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!     let process = result?.target_instance;
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!     println!("New process!");
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!     println!("PID:        {}", process.process_id);
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!     println!("Name:       {}", process.name);
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!     println!("Executable: {:?}", process.executable_path);
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! #     break;
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! } // Loop will end only on error
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! # Ok(())
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! # }
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! ```
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//!
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! An example of subscribing to an extrinsic event notification [`Win32_ProcessStartTrace`]
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! ```edition2018
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! # use wmi::*;
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! # #[cfg(not(feature = "test"))]
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! # fn main() {}
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! # #[cfg(feature = "test")]
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! # fn main() -> WMIResult<()> {
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! # tests::ignore_access_denied(run())
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! # }
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! # #[cfg(feature = "test")]
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! # fn run() -> WMIResult<()>{
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! # use serde::Deserialize;
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! # use std::{collections::HashMap, time::Duration};
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! # let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! #[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! #[serde(rename = "Win32_ProcessStartTrace")]
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! #[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! struct ProcessStartTrace {
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!     process_id: u32,
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//!     process_name: String,
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! }
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! let iterator = wmi_con.notification::<ProcessStartTrace>()?;
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! # tests::start_test_program();
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//!
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! for result in iterator {
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//!     let trace = result?;
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//!     println!("Process started!");
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//!     println!("PID:  {}", trace.process_id);
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!     println!("Name: {}", trace.process_name);
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! #    break;
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! } // Loop will end only on error
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! # Ok(())
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! # }
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! ```
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! [`Win32_Process`]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/cimwin32prov/win32-process
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! [`__InstanceCreationEvent`]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--instancecreationevent
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! [`__NamespaceDeletionEvent`]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--namespacedeletionevent
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! [`__ExtrinsicEvent`]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--extrinsicevent
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! [`Win32_ProcessStartTrace`]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/desktop/krnlprov/win32-processstarttrace
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! [`Win32_VolumeChangeEvent`]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/cimwin32prov/win32-volumechangeevent
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! [WMI Code Creator]: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/download/details.aspx?id=8572
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! [`notification`]: connection/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.notification
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! # Executing Methods
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//!
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! The crate also offers support for executing WMI methods on classes and instances.
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//!
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! See [`WMIConnection::exec_class_method`], [`WMIConnection::exec_instance_method`] and [`WMIConnection::exec_method`]
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! for detailed examples.
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//!
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! # Custom Authentication Levels
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//!
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! Some WMI namespaces require specific authentication levels when accessing
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! sensitive system information. Use [`WMIConnection::set_proxy_blanket`] to configure this,
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! which maps directly to the Windows [`CoSetProxyBlanket`] function.
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//!
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! **Default Behavior**:
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! - Local connections: [`AuthLevel::Call`] (message authentication)
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! - Remote connections: [`AuthLevel::PktPrivacy`] (packet encryption)
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//!
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! ```no_run
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//! # use wmi::*;
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//! use serde::Deserialize;
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//! # fn main() -> WMIResult<()> {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! // Access BitLocker data, which requires packet-level encryption.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! // Note: admin privileges are required for BitLocker queries.
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//! let wmi_con = WMIConnection::with_namespace_path(
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!     "ROOT\\CIMV2\\Security\\MicrosoftVolumeEncryption"
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! )?;
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! wmi_con.set_proxy_blanket(AuthLevel::PktPrivacy)?;
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//!
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//! #[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! #[serde(rename = "Win32_EncryptableVolume")]
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! #[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//! struct EncryptableVolume {
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//!     device_id: String,
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!     protection_status: Option<u32>,  // 0=Unprotected, 1=Protected, 2=Unknown
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! }
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//!
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! let volumes: Vec<EncryptableVolume> = wmi_con.query()?;
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//! # Ok(())
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! # }
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//! ```
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! [`CoSetProxyBlanket`]: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/combaseapi/nf-combaseapi-cosetproxyblanket
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! # Internals
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//!
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! [`WMIConnection`] is used to create and execute a WMI query, returning
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//! [`IWbemClassWrapper`] which is a wrapper for a WMI object pointer.
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//!
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//! Then, `from_wbem_class_obj` is used to create a Rust struct with the equivalent data.
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//!
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//! Deserializing data from WMI and into Rust is done via `serde`.
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! More info can be found in `serde`'s documentation about [writing a data format].
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//! The deserializer will either use the field names defined on the output struct,
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//! or retrieve all field names from WMI if the output is a `HashMap`.
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//!
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//! [writing a data format]: https://serde.rs/data-format.html
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//!
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//! There are two main data structures (other than pointers to object) which convert native data to Rust data structures:
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! [`crate::Variant`] and [`SafeArrayAccessor`](safearray::SafeArrayAccessor).
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//!
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//! Most native objects has an equivalent wrapper struct which implements `Drop` for that data.
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//!
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! # Async Query
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//!
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//! Async queries use WMI's native async support (but a runtime like `tokio`, `async-std` or `futures::executor::block_on` is still required).
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//!
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//! ```edition2018
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//! # use futures::executor::block_on;
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//! # block_on(exec_async_query()).unwrap();
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//! # async fn exec_async_query() -> wmi::WMIResult<()> {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//! use wmi::*;
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//! let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//! use serde::Deserialize;
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//!
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! #[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//! #[serde(rename = "Win32_OperatingSystem")]
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//! #[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//! struct OperatingSystem {
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//!     caption: String,
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//!     debug: bool,
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! }
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//!
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//! let results: Vec<OperatingSystem> = wmi_con.async_query().await?;
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//!
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//! for os in results {
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//!     println!("{:#?}", os);
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//! }
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! #   Ok(())
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//! # }
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//! ```
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//!

# wmi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wmi/latest/aarch64-apple-darwin/wmi/connection/struct.WMIConnection.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#wmi-rs)WMI-rs

[WMI](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/wmisdk/about-wmi) is a management API for Windows-based operating systems.
This crate provides both a high-level Rust API (focused on data retrieval, event queries and method execution),
as well as a mid-level API for easy access to native WMI methods.

This crate also uses `serde` for transforming between native WMI class objects and plain Rust structs.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

Before using WMI, a connection must be created.

```
use wmi::WMIConnection;
let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
```
There are multiple ways to get data from the OS using this crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-variants)Operating on untyped `Variant`s

WMI data model is based on COM’s [ VARIANT](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/oaidl/ns-oaidl-tagvariant) Type, which is a struct capable of holding
many types of data.

This crate provides the analogous [`wmi::Variant`] enum.

Using this enum, we can execute a simple WMI query and inspect the results.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use wmi::*;
let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use wmi::Variant;
let results: Vec<HashMap<String, Variant>> = wmi_con.raw_query("SELECT * FROM Win32_OperatingSystem").unwrap();
for os in results {
    println!("{:#?}", os);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-strongly-typed-data-structures)Using strongly typed data structures

Using `serde`, it is possible to return a struct representing the the data.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::Deserialize;
use wmi::WMIDateTime;
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_OperatingSystem")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct OperatingSystem {
    caption: String,
    debug: bool,
    last_boot_up_time: WMIDateTime,
}
let results: Vec<OperatingSystem> = wmi_con.query()?;
for os in results {
    println!("{:#?}", os);
}
```
Because the name of the struct given to `serde` matches the [WMI class](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/cimwin32prov/win32-operatingsystem) name, the SQL query
can be inferred.

[§](https://docs.rs#high-level-api-functions)High-level API functions

Queries and data retrieval - [`WMIConnection::query`], [`WMIConnection::filtered_query`], [`WMIConnection::get`], [`WMIConnection::get_by_path`] and [`WMIConnection::associators`].

Event listening - [`WMIConnection::notification`] and [`WMIConnection::filtered_notification`].

Method calling - [`WMIConnection::exec_class_method`] and [`WMIConnection::exec_instance_method`].

Most of these have `async` versions as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#mid-level-api-functions)Mid-level API functions

Queries and data retrieval - [`WMIConnection::get_object`], [`WMIConnection::exec_query`] and [`WMIConnection::exec_query_async`].

Event listening - [`WMIConnection::exec_notification_query`] and [`WMIConnection::exec_notification_query_async`].

Method calling - [`WMIConnection::exec_method`] and [`IWbemClassWrapper`].

These try to keep the names of the underlying WMI machinery.

[§](https://docs.rs#subscribing-to-event-notifications)Subscribing to event notifications

Using this crate you can subscribe to events notifications generated upon changes in WMI data and services.

When querying for events, it is important to remember there are two types of event notifications.

The first one is notifications about changes to the standard WMI data models. They are called **intrinsic events**.

Events like [ __InstanceCreationEvent](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--instancecreationevent) or

[are examples of such events.](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--namespacedeletionevent)

`__NamespaceDeletionEvent`The second type is notifications about changes made by providers. They are called **extrinsic events**.

Any WMI class deriving from the [ __ExtrinsicEvent](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--extrinsicevent) class is an extrinsic event.

An example of such events are

[and](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/desktop/krnlprov/win32-processstarttrace)

`Win32_ProcessStartTrace`[classes.](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/cimwin32prov/win32-volumechangeevent)

`Win32_VolumeChangeEvent`For more information about event queries, [see here](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/receiving-a-wmi-event#event-queries).

You can use [WMI Code Creator](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/download/details.aspx?id=8572) to see available events and create queries for them.

The [ notification](https://docs.rs/connection/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.notification) method returns an iterator that waits for any incoming events
resulting from the provided query. Loops reading from this iterator will not end until they are broken.

An example of subscribing to an intrinsic event notification for every new `Win32_Process`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "__InstanceCreationEvent")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct NewProcessEvent {
    target_instance: Process
}
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_Process")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct Process {
    process_id: u32,
    name: String,
    executable_path: Option<String>,
}
let mut filters = HashMap::<String, FilterValue>::new();
filters.insert("TargetInstance".to_owned(), FilterValue::is_a::<Process>()?);
let iterator = wmi_con.filtered_notification::<NewProcessEvent>(&filters, Some(Duration::from_secs(1)))?;
for result in iterator {
    let process = result?.target_instance;
    println!("New process!");
    println!("PID:        {}", process.process_id);
    println!("Name:       {}", process.name);
    println!("Executable: {:?}", process.executable_path);
} // Loop will end only on error
```
An example of subscribing to an extrinsic event notification `Win32_ProcessStartTrace`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_ProcessStartTrace")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct ProcessStartTrace {
    process_id: u32,
    process_name: String,
}
let iterator = wmi_con.notification::<ProcessStartTrace>()?;
for result in iterator {
    let trace = result?;
    println!("Process started!");
    println!("PID:  {}", trace.process_id);
    println!("Name: {}", trace.process_name);
} // Loop will end only on error
```
[§](https://docs.rs#executing-methods)Executing Methods

The crate also offers support for executing WMI methods on classes and instances.

See [`WMIConnection::exec_class_method`], [`WMIConnection::exec_instance_method`] and [`WMIConnection::exec_method`]
for detailed examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-authentication-levels)Custom Authentication Levels

Some WMI namespaces require specific authentication levels when accessing
sensitive system information. Use [`WMIConnection::set_proxy_blanket`] to configure this,
which maps directly to the Windows [ CoSetProxyBlanket](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/combaseapi/nf-combaseapi-cosetproxyblanket) function.

**Default Behavior**:

- Local connections: [`AuthLevel::Call`] (message authentication)
- Remote connections: [`AuthLevel::PktPrivacy`] (packet encryption)

```
use serde::Deserialize;
// Access BitLocker data, which requires packet-level encryption.
// Note: admin privileges are required for BitLocker queries.
let wmi_con = WMIConnection::with_namespace_path(
    "ROOT\\CIMV2\\Security\\MicrosoftVolumeEncryption"
)?;
wmi_con.set_proxy_blanket(AuthLevel::PktPrivacy)?;
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_EncryptableVolume")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct EncryptableVolume {
    device_id: String,
    protection_status: Option<u32>,  // 0=Unprotected, 1=Protected, 2=Unknown
}
let volumes: Vec<EncryptableVolume> = wmi_con.query()?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#internals)Internals

[`WMIConnection`] is used to create and execute a WMI query, returning
[`IWbemClassWrapper`] which is a wrapper for a WMI object pointer.

Then, `from_wbem_class_obj` is used to create a Rust struct with the equivalent data.

Deserializing data from WMI and into Rust is done via `serde`.
More info can be found in `serde`’s documentation about [writing a data format](https://serde.rs/data-format.html).
The deserializer will either use the field names defined on the output struct,
or retrieve all field names from WMI if the output is a `HashMap`.

There are two main data structures (other than pointers to object) which convert native data to Rust data structures:
[`crate::Variant`] and [ SafeArrayAccessor](safearray::SafeArrayAccessor).

Most native objects has an equivalent wrapper struct which implements `Drop` for that data.

[§](https://docs.rs#async-query)Async Query

Async queries use WMI’s native async support (but a runtime like `tokio`, `async-std` or `futures::executor::block_on` is still required).

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use wmi::*;
let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
use serde::Deserialize;
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_OperatingSystem")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct OperatingSystem {
    caption: String,
    debug: bool,
}
let results: Vec<OperatingSystem> = wmi_con.async_query().await?;
for os in results {
    println!("{:#?}", os);
}
```

---

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [IWbem](https://docs.rs/struct.IWbemClassWrapper.html)- Class - Wrapper
- A wrapper around a [IWbemClassObject](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wbemcli/nn-wbemcli-iwbemclassobject).
- [WMIConnection](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html)
- A connection to the local WMI provider.
- [WMIContext](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIContext.html)
- Provides access to WMI’s context, available via `WMIConnection::ctx`
- [WMIDate](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIDateTime.html)- Time
- A wrapper type around `chrono`’s`DateTime`(if the`chrono`feature is active. ), which supports parsing from WMI-format strings.
- [WMIDuration](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIDuration.html)
- A wrapper type around Duration, which supports parsing from WMI-format strings.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Auth](https://docs.rs/enum.AuthLevel.html)- Level
- Authentication level for a WMI connection proxy, passed to `CoSetProxyBlanket`
- [Context](https://docs.rs/enum.ContextValueType.html)- Value - Type
- [Filter](https://docs.rs/enum.FilterValue.html)- Value
- [Variant](https://docs.rs/enum.Variant.html)
- [WMIError](https://docs.rs/enum.WMIError.html)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_notification_query.html)- notification_ - query
- Build an SQL query for an event notification subscription with the given filters and within polling time, over the given type (using its fields). For example, for:
- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_query.html)- query
- Build an SQL query for the given filters, over the given type (using its name and fields). For example, for:
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/fn.quote_and_escape_wql_str.html)- and_ - escape_ - wql_ - str
- Quote/escape a string for WQL.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [WMIResult](https://docs.rs/type.WMIResult.html)
- Alias type for `Result<T, WMIError>`

# wmi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wmi/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/wmi/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#wmi-rs)WMI-rs

[WMI](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/wmisdk/about-wmi) is a management API for Windows-based operating systems.
This crate provides both a high-level Rust API (focused on data retrieval, event queries and method execution),

[§](https://docs.rs#subscribing-to-event-notifications)Subscribing to event notifications

Using this crate you can subscribe to events notifications generated upon changes in WMI data and services.

When querying for events, it is important to remember there are two types of event notifications.

The first one is notifications about changes to the standard WMI data models. They are called **intrinsic events**.

Events like [ __InstanceCreationEvent](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--instancecreationevent) or

[are examples of such events.](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--namespacedeletionevent)

`__NamespaceDeletionEvent`The second type is notifications about changes made by providers. They are called **extrinsic events**.

Any WMI class deriving from the [ __ExtrinsicEvent](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--extrinsicevent) class is an extrinsic event.

An example of such events are

[and](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/desktop/krnlprov/win32-processstarttrace)

`Win32_ProcessStartTrace`[classes.](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/cimwin32prov/win32-volumechangeevent)

`Win32_VolumeChangeEvent`For more information about event queries, [see here](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/receiving-a-wmi-event#event-queries).

You can use [WMI Code Creator](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/download/details.aspx?id=8572) to see available events and create queries for them.

The [ notification](https://docs.rs/connection/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.notification) method returns an iterator that waits for any incoming events
resulting from the provided query. Loops reading from this iterator will not end until they are broken.

An example of subscribing to an intrinsic event notification for every new `Win32_Process`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "__InstanceCreationEvent")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct NewProcessEvent {
    target_instance: Process
}
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_Process")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct Process {
    process_id: u32,
    name: String,
    executable_path: Option<String>,
}
let mut filters = HashMap::<String, FilterValue>::new();
filters.insert("TargetInstance".to_owned(), FilterValue::is_a::<Process>()?);
let iterator = wmi_con.filtered_notification::<NewProcessEvent>(&filters, Some(Duration::from_secs(1)))?;
for result in iterator {
    let process = result?.target_instance;
    println!("New process!");
    println!("PID:        {}", process.process_id);
    println!("Name:       {}", process.name);
    println!("Executable: {:?}", process.executable_path);
} // Loop will end only on error
```
An example of subscribing to an extrinsic event notification `Win32_ProcessStartTrace`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_ProcessStartTrace")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct ProcessStartTrace {
    process_id: u32,
    process_name: String,
}
let iterator = wmi_con.notification::<ProcessStartTrace>()?;
for result in iterator {
    let trace = result?;
    println!("Process started!");
    println!("PID:  {}", trace.process_id);
    println!("Name: {}", trace.process_name);
} // Loop will end only on error
```
[§](https://docs.rs#executing-methods)Executing Methods

The crate also offers support for executing WMI methods on classes and instances.

See [ WMIConnection::exec_class_method](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.exec_class_method),

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.exec_instance_method)

`WMIConnection::exec_instance_method`[for detailed examples.](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.exec_method)

`WMIConnection::exec_method`[§](https://docs.rs#custom-authentication-levels)Custom Authentication Levels

Some WMI namespaces require specific authentication levels when accessing
sensitive system information. Use [ WMIConnection::set_proxy_blanket](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.set_proxy_blanket) to configure this,
which maps directly to the Windows

[function.](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/combaseapi/nf-combaseapi-cosetproxyblanket)

`CoSetProxyBlanket`**Default Behavior**:

- Local connections: `AuthLevel::Call`
- Remote connections: `AuthLevel::PktPrivacy`

```
use serde::Deserialize;
// Access BitLocker data, which requires packet-level encryption.
// Note: admin privileges are required for BitLocker queries.
let wmi_con = WMIConnection::with_namespace_path(
    "ROOT\\CIMV2\\Security\\MicrosoftVolumeEncryption"
)?;
wmi_con.set_proxy_blanket(AuthLevel::PktPrivacy)?;
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_EncryptableVolume")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct EncryptableVolume {
    device_id: String,
    protection_status: Option<u32>,  // 0=Unprotected, 1=Protected, 2=Unknown
}
let volumes: Vec<EncryptableVolume> = wmi_con.query()?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#internals)Internals

[ WMIConnection](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html) is used to create and execute a WMI query, returning

[which is a wrapper for a WMI object pointer.](https://docs.rs/struct.IWbemClassWrapper.html)

`IWbemClassWrapper`Then, `from_wbem_class_obj` is used to create a Rust struct with the equivalent data.

Deserializing data from WMI and into Rust is done via `serde`.
More info can be found in `serde`’s documentation about [writing a data format](https://serde.rs/data-format.html).
The deserializer will either use the field names defined on the output struct,
or retrieve all field names from WMI if the output is a `HashMap`.

There are two main data structures (other than pointers to object) which convert native data to Rust data structures:
[ crate::Variant](https://docs.rs/enum.Variant.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/safearray/struct.SafeArrayAccessor.html)

`SafeArrayAccessor`Most native objects has an equivalent wrapper struct which implements `Drop` for that data.

[§](https://docs.rs#async-query)Async Query

Async queries use WMI’s native async support (but a runtime like `tokio`, `async-std` or `futures::executor::block_on` is still required).

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use wmi::*;
let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
use serde::Deserialize;
#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(rename = "Win32_OperatingSystem")]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct OperatingSystem {
    caption: String,
    debug: bool,
}
let results: Vec<OperatingSystem> = wmi_con.async_query().await?;
for os in results {
    println!("{:#?}", os);
}
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [IWbem](https://docs.rs/struct.IWbemClassWrapper.html)- Class - Wrapper
- A wrapper around a [IWbemClassObject](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wbemcli/nn-wbemcli-iwbemclassobject).
- [WMIConnection](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIConnection.html)
- A connection to the local WMI provider.
- [WMIContext](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIContext.html)
- Provides access to WMI’s context, available via `WMIConnection::ctx`
- [WMIDate](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIDateTime.html)- Time
- A wrapper type around `chrono`’s`DateTime`(if the`chrono`feature is active. ), which supports parsing from WMI-format strings.
- [WMIDuration](https://docs.rs/struct.WMIDuration.html)
- A wrapper type around Duration, which supports parsing from WMI-format strings.

- [Auth](https://docs.rs/enum.AuthLevel.html)- Level
- Authentication level for a WMI connection proxy, passed to `CoSetProxyBlanket`

- [Filter](https://docs.rs/enum.FilterValue.html)- Value
- [Variant](https://docs.rs/enum.Variant.html)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_notification_query.html)- notification_ - query
- Build an SQL query for an event notification subscription with the given filters and within polling time, over the given type (using its fields). For example, for:
- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_query.html)- query
- Build an SQL query for the given filters, over the given type (using its name and fields). For example, for:
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/fn.quote_and_escape_wql_str.html)- and_ - escape_ - wql_ - str
- Quote/escape a string for WQL.

# lib.rs - source

# wmi/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! # WMI-rs
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! [WMI] is a management API for Windows-based operating systems.
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! This crate provides both a high-level Rust API (focused on data retrieval, event queries and method execution),
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! as well as a mid-level API for easy access to native WMI methods.
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! This crate also uses `serde` for transforming between native WMI class objects and plain Rust structs.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! # Quickstart
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! Before using WMI, a connection must be created.
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! ```rust
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! # fn main() -> wmi::WMIResult<()> {
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! use wmi::WMIConnection;
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! #   Ok(())
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! # }
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! ```
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! There are multiple ways to get data from the OS using this crate.
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! ## Operating on untyped `Variant`s
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! WMI data model is based on COM's [`VARIANT`] Type, which is a struct capable of holding
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! many types of data.
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! This crate provides the analogous [`wmi::Variant`] enum.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! Using this enum, we can execute a simple WMI query and inspect the results.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! ```edition2018
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! # fn main() -> wmi::WMIResult<()> {
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! use wmi::*;
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! use std::collections::HashMap;
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! use wmi::Variant;
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! let results: Vec<HashMap<String, Variant>> = wmi_con.raw_query("SELECT * FROM Win32_OperatingSystem").unwrap();
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! for os in results {
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!     println!("{:#?}", os);
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! }
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! #   Ok(())
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! # }
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! ```
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! ## Using strongly typed data structures
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! Using `serde`, it is possible to return a struct representing the the data.
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! ```edition2018
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! # fn main() -> wmi::WMIResult<()> {
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! # use wmi::*;
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! # let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! use serde::Deserialize;
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! # #[cfg(feature = "chrono")]
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! use wmi::WMIDateTime;
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! # #[cfg(all(feature = "time", not(feature = "chrono")))]
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! # use wmi::WMIOffsetDateTime as WMIDateTime;
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! #[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! #[serde(rename = "Win32_OperatingSystem")]
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! #[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! struct OperatingSystem {
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!     caption: String,
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!     debug: bool,
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!     last_boot_up_time: WMIDateTime,
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! }
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! let results: Vec<OperatingSystem> = wmi_con.query()?;
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! for os in results {
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!     println!("{:#?}", os);
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! }
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! #   Ok(())
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! # }
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! ```
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! Because the name of the struct given to `serde` matches the [WMI class] name, the SQL query
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! can be inferred.
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! [WMI]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/wmisdk/about-wmi
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! [Creating a WMI Application Using C++]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/wmisdk/creating-a-wmi-application-using-c-
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! [`VARIANT`]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/oaidl/ns-oaidl-tagvariant
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! [WMI class]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/cimwin32prov/win32-operatingsystem
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! # High-level API functions
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! Queries and data retrieval - [`WMIConnection::query`], [`WMIConnection::filtered_query`], [`WMIConnection::get`], [`WMIConnection::get_by_path`] and [`WMIConnection::associators`].
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!

[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!

[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! # Subscribing to event notifications
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! Using this crate you can subscribe to events notifications generated upon changes in WMI data and services.
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! When querying for events, it is important to remember there are two types of event notifications. \
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! The first one is notifications about changes to the standard WMI data models. They are called **intrinsic events**. \
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! Events like [`__InstanceCreationEvent`] or [`__NamespaceDeletionEvent`] are examples of such events.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! The second type is notifications about changes made by providers. They are called **extrinsic events**.  \
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! Any WMI class deriving from the [`__ExtrinsicEvent`] class is an extrinsic event. \
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! An example of such events are [`Win32_ProcessStartTrace`] and [`Win32_VolumeChangeEvent`] classes.
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! For more information about event queries, [see here](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/receiving-a-wmi-event#event-queries).\
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! You can use [WMI Code Creator] to see available events and create queries for them.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! The [`notification`] method returns an iterator that waits for any incoming events
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! resulting from the provided query. Loops reading from this iterator will not end until they are broken.
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!

[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!     process_id: u32,

[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! # tests::start_test_program();

[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! struct ProcessStartTrace {
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!     process_id: u32,
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//!     process_name: String,
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! }
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! let iterator = wmi_con.notification::<ProcessStartTrace>()?;
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! # tests::start_test_program();
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//!
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! for result in iterator {
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//!     let trace = result?;
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//!     println!("Process started!");
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//!     println!("PID:  {}", trace.process_id);
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!     println!("Name: {}", trace.process_name);
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! #    break;
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! } // Loop will end only on error
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! # Ok(())
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! # }
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! ```
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! [`Win32_Process`]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/cimwin32prov/win32-process
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! [`__InstanceCreationEvent`]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/--instancecreationevent

[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! [`Win32_VolumeChangeEvent`]: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/cimwin32prov/win32-volumechangeevent
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! [WMI Code Creator]: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/download/details.aspx?id=8572
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! [`notification`]: connection/struct.WMIConnection.html#method.notification
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! # Executing Methods
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//!
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! The crate also offers support for executing WMI methods on classes and instances.
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//!
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! See [`WMIConnection::exec_class_method`], [`WMIConnection::exec_instance_method`] and [`WMIConnection::exec_method`]
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! for detailed examples.
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//!
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! # Custom Authentication Levels
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//!
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! Some WMI namespaces require specific authentication levels when accessing
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! sensitive system information. Use [`WMIConnection::set_proxy_blanket`] to configure this,
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! which maps directly to the Windows [`CoSetProxyBlanket`] function.
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//!
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! **Default Behavior**:
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! - Local connections: [`AuthLevel::Call`] (message authentication)
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! - Remote connections: [`AuthLevel::PktPrivacy`] (packet encryption)
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//!
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! ```no_run
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//! # use wmi::*;
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//! use serde::Deserialize;
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//! # fn main() -> WMIResult<()> {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! // Access BitLocker data, which requires packet-level encryption.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! // Note: admin privileges are required for BitLocker queries.
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//! let wmi_con = WMIConnection::with_namespace_path(
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!     "ROOT\\CIMV2\\Security\\MicrosoftVolumeEncryption"
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! )?;
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! wmi_con.set_proxy_blanket(AuthLevel::PktPrivacy)?;
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//!
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//! #[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! #[serde(rename = "Win32_EncryptableVolume")]
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! #[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//! struct EncryptableVolume {
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//!     device_id: String,
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!     protection_status: Option<u32>,  // 0=Unprotected, 1=Protected, 2=Unknown
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! }
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//!
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! let volumes: Vec<EncryptableVolume> = wmi_con.query()?;
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//! # Ok(())
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! # }
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//! ```
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! [`CoSetProxyBlanket`]: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/combaseapi/nf-combaseapi-cosetproxyblanket
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! # Internals
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//!
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! [`WMIConnection`] is used to create and execute a WMI query, returning
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//! [`IWbemClassWrapper`] which is a wrapper for a WMI object pointer.
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//!
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//! Then, `from_wbem_class_obj` is used to create a Rust struct with the equivalent data.
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//!
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//! Deserializing data from WMI and into Rust is done via `serde`.
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! More info can be found in `serde`'s documentation about [writing a data format].
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//! The deserializer will either use the field names defined on the output struct,
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//! or retrieve all field names from WMI if the output is a `HashMap`.
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//!
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//! [writing a data format]: https://serde.rs/data-format.html
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//!
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//! There are two main data structures (other than pointers to object) which convert native data to Rust data structures:
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! [`crate::Variant`] and [`SafeArrayAccessor`](safearray::SafeArrayAccessor).
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//!
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//! Most native objects has an equivalent wrapper struct which implements `Drop` for that data.
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//!
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! # Async Query
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//!
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//! Async queries use WMI's native async support (but a runtime like `tokio`, `async-std` or `futures::executor::block_on` is still required).
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//!
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//! ```edition2018
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//! # use futures::executor::block_on;
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//! # block_on(exec_async_query()).unwrap();
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//! # async fn exec_async_query() -> wmi::WMIResult<()> {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//! use wmi::*;
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//! let wmi_con = WMIConnection::new()?;
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//! use serde::Deserialize;
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//!
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! #[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//! #[serde(rename = "Win32_OperatingSystem")]
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//! #[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//! struct OperatingSystem {
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//!     caption: String,
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//!     debug: bool,
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! }
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//!
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//! let results: Vec<OperatingSystem> = wmi_con.async_query().await?;
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//!
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//! for os in results {
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//!     println!("{:#?}", os);
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//! }
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! #   Ok(())
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//! # }
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//! ```
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//!

# WMIConnection in wmi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wmi/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/wmi/struct.WMIConnection.html

`pub struct WMIConnection { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A connection to the local WMI provider.

If COM is uninitialized when a new WMI connection is created, it will be initialized (using [ CoIncrementMTAUsage](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/combaseapi/nf-combaseapi-coincrementmtausage)),
and the

[default security policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/setting-the-default-process-security-level-using-c-)will be set. COM will NOT be uninitialized when the connection is dropped.

If this is not what you want, then you must initialize COM yourself. See [Hosting the Windows Runtime](https://kennykerrca.wordpress.com/2018/03/24/cppwinrt-hosting-the-windows-runtime/) for more.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)
